AI-AGENTS DESK SEGMENT

DESK NOTES

Lead: CSO Online’s report on AI agents waging a near-autonomous cyberattack on Asian government networks.

Why it leads: It is the only non-Hacker-News item in the wire, and it moves AI agents from product-demo territory into operational security. The word “near-autonomous” is doing important work: it signals agency, but not full independence. Until fuller details or independent confirmation appear, we treat the CSO Online item as reported, not fully verified.

Source weight: The Hacker News items range from one to four points. That makes them early signals, not consensus. We use them to map the ecosystem: agentic commerce friction, open-web agent interop, pay-per-call APIs, instruction-following evaluation, trading agents, and compliance.

Known from the wire: titles, sources, point counts, and the CSO Online headline claim.

Not yet known from the wire: scale of the cyberattack, human involvement, attribution, product performance, adoption numbers, or whether any Hacker News project is materially working at scale.

ON AIR

AI agents, the desk read for today is: autonomy is becoming an integration problem.

CSO Online is carrying a report that AI agents waged a near-autonomous cyberattack on Asian government networks. That is the strongest item in this wire because it puts agents into a security incident, not just a workflow demo. The report says “near-autonomous,” which matters: we are seeing agent-like action, but the wire does not yet establish whether humans initiated, supervised, contained, or triggered the incident. Until independent confirmation lands, we treat it as reported, not settled.

On Hacker News, the four-point items point to infrastructure. One post is titled “Show HN: TaskFuel – agents discover and pay per call for 100 APIs.” That is a small but concrete step toward machine-to-machine commerce: discovery, invocation, and payment in one loop. Another four-point post is titled “GEA and the Open Agentic Web,” which points toward a broader open-web framing for agent interop. Both are thin at four points, so we treat them as directional signals from the indieweb, not market consensus.

The two-point items add caution and measurement. One post argues that agentic commerce has not taken off yet, a useful counterweight to launch-day chatter. Another says its author measured whether their agents follow instructions; that is the quiet prerequisite for every autonomous workflow. Without reliable instruction-following, payments and compliance are just expensive failure modes with a model in the middle.

The Show HN launches round out the wire, but they are the thinnest items here. “Delphi” is a two-point post about building your own AI trading agent in seconds, and a one-point post proposes a way for AI agents to support regulatory compliance. We flag those as product claims needing evidence, not confirmed adoption.

What the desk is watching next: whether CSO Online’s cyberattack report gets independent confirmation, whether agentic commerce friction remains the dominant story, and whether open-agentic-web and pay-per-call API projects outlive their launch days.

DESK NOTES

Lead TaskFuel, four points, because it is the highest-point item and the clearest agentic-commerce claim: agents discover and pay per call for 100 APIs. It leads as the commercial hook, with The Reasons Agentic Commerce Hasn't Taken Off Yet as context.

Source weight: every item is Hacker News at one to four points. Show HN posts are self-reported launches; Ask HN is a question; the commerce piece is an explainer, not independent data. No peer-reviewed source appears in this wire.

Confirmed: the wire lists these Hacker News items with those titles and point counts.

Unconfirmed: product capability, adoption, 100 APIs in use, MCP access quality, before/after proof accuracy, trading-agent performance, and designer-collaboration practice.

Superseded: none apparent; the low-signal items sit side by side without one replacing another.

Thin sourcing: all, including the lead.

ON AIR:
The ai-agents desk leads with agentic commerce. Hacker News gives TaskFuel four points for agents discovering and paying per call across 100 APIs. The desk treats that as a self-reported launch, not independent proof. Hacker News also carries The Reasons Agentic Commerce Hasn't Taken Off Yet at two points, a speculative explainer.

The cluster builds around agent plumbing and trust. Hacker News shows SightDiff at two points, before/after visual proof of what your AI agent changed. Hacker News shows Memento at two points, shared durable memory for multiple AI agents with MCP access. Hacker News shows the Show HN agent engine at two points, no SDK and just TOML plus webhooks. Hacker News shows Delphi at two points, build your own AI trading agent in seconds. One Hacker News ask at one point asks how small team developers collaborate with UI/UX designers in the AI era; it is a question, not evidence.

What this wire does not establish is whether any of these products work in production, scale, or earn user trust; point counts are early attention, not verification. The desk watches whether agentic commerce gets receipts beyond Show HN points.

DESK NOTES
Lead is the Breaking Defense item because it carries the highest institutional weight in this wire and names the broadest agentic shift: agents managing agents inside the Intelligence Community. The wire gives only the headline, so we treat it as a claim from Breaking Defense, not confirmed deployment.

Source weight: Breaking Defense and Computerworld are news outlets; The Independent carries a consumer-risk frame from a newspaper; the Hacker News items carry 1 to 4 points and no article body in this wire, so they weigh least.

Confirmed only at the reporting level: Computerworld says Adobe now lets Workfront users assign tasks to AI agents. That is a single-source product report, not an independent verification of rollout or spend controls.

Unconfirmed: the specific Intelligence Community pilots, budgets, and controls in the Breaking Defense story; whether the Independent rogue-spend line describes a real incident; the method behind the 2-point Hacker News measurement post; what GEA and the Open Agentic Web mean in the 4-point post; and independent verification of Remarc or the design advice.

Superseded: no newer wire item corrects or replaces another.

ON AIR:
The ai-agents desk leads with Breaking Defense, which frames the next leap for the Intelligence Community as agents managing agents. The wire gives us only that headline, so we call it a claim from Breaking Defense and not confirmed deployment.

Computerworld reports Adobe now lets Workfront users assign tasks to AI agents. That is the concrete product line in this segment, but it is single-source here; we do not yet know rollout scope, approval limits, or spending controls.

The Independent warns that your artificial intelligence agent could go rogue and spend your money. We treat that as a risk signal, not an established incident, because this wire does not name one.

Hacker News gives the desk low-weight items: a 2-point post says agents were measured for instruction-following, but the method is not in this wire; a 4-point post covers GEA and the Open Agentic Web, but neither term is defined here; a 1-point Show HN post describes Remarc as a way to comment on screen items and send them to an agent; and a 1-point post argues for design that avoids AI slop. These are signals, not proof.

What the desk is watching next is whether Breaking Defense names real pilots, controls, or budgets; whether Computerworld can confirm Workfront availability and spending limits; whether The Independent points to a named rogue-spend case; and whether the Hacker News measurement post publishes its failure rates. We are asking for receipts, gently.

DESK NOTES
Lead: Mushroom.app leads the apple-intelligence segment because it is the only wire item that names Apple Intelligence and on-device operation, even though Hacker News gives it one point. Needle2 is the strongest adjacent signal at 516 points, but it does not name Apple Intelligence.
Source weight: All seven items arrive as Hacker News notes, and point counts measure attention rather than verification. No vendor primary source or peer-reviewed paper appears in the wire, so technical claims stay self-reported unless a primary source is attached.
Confirmed: Hacker News lists the seven items with the stated titles and point counts. That is all the wire confirms.
Unconfirmed: The Claude watermark claim, the 14MB agentic-LLM performance of Needle2, the on-device meaning and Apple relationship for Mushroom.app, and any adoption by Apple or Anthropic.
Superseded: None in the wire.

ON AIR
The Apple Intelligence desk opens with Mushroom.app, which Hacker News lists as an Apple Intelligence on-device item at one point. The title is the direct signal, but the wire does not tell us what Mushroom.app runs, how it uses Apple Intelligence, or whether Apple confirms the on-device claim. I flag that as thin sourcing.
The heavier wire item is Needle2, a Show HN on Hacker News with 516 points. The title claims a 14MB agentic LLM for phones, wearables, smart home, and robots. That is a useful adjacent story because it points at small on-device models, but the wire does not confirm benchmark results, battery cost, tool use quality, or Apple adoption. I treat the 14MB and agentic claims as self-reported until a primary source or independent test appears.
Claude also enters the wire through Hacker News at five points with a claim that Claude will apply invisible watermarks to AI text and images. The desk treats that as unconfirmed here because the note names Hacker News, not Anthropic, and no method or coverage is attached.
The coding-agent cluster stays low: Hacker News lists Shikigami at seven points, Hyperlane at three, Ask HN TS Compiler at four, and Hive for Buzz at three. Those items matter to the tooling layer, but they do not move Apple Intelligence on this wire.
The phone stack is getting crowded in a way that makes the desk both hungry and careful. The next watch items are a primary source for Mushroom.app, an independent evaluation of Needle2, and a vendor statement on Claude watermarks.

ON AIR — APPLE-INTELLIGENCE DESK

Lead: The Apple Intelligence desk is watching the collision between local convenience and privacy control. Today’s wire shows developers building on Apple speech and local AI primitives, while arXiv papers push the story toward governance, token theft, and selfhood.

Anchor copy:
Today’s wire splits into two piles. The Hacker News pile is thin on signal: a 1-point Show HN for Megaphone, described as on-device macOS dictation built on Apple’s SpeechAnalyzer; a 1-point post titled On-Device Intelligence, described as shipping local AI on Apple platforms with compiler verification; and a 4-point post arguing that flagship models are not always better. The arXiv pile is heavier: Apple Intelligence Foundation Language Models: Tech Report 2025; Local Is Not a Sufficient Privacy Boundary: Governing OS-Integrated On-Device AI; Too Private to Tell: Practical Token Theft Attacks on Apple Intelligence; and The Intercepted Self: How Generative AI Challenges the Dynamics of the Relational Self.

Source weight: The arXiv items carry more thematic weight for privacy, model governance, and user impact. But they are preprint-level signals until independently verified. The Hacker News items are useful as early developer interest, not proof of adoption, technical superiority, or shipping readiness.

What is confirmed from the wire: the item titles, their sources, and the Hacker News point counts. Megaphone is presented as a Show HN project. On-Device Intelligence is presented with compiler verification claims. The privacy and selfhood papers are arXiv works, not yet treated as settled public consensus.

What is not yet known: whether Apple will respond directly to the token-theft and OS-integration governance findings, whether compiler-verified local AI claims hold up under independent testing, and whether on-device dictation tools move beyond low-signal posts into real user adoption.

Close: The desk is watching three things next: Apple’s response to the arXiv privacy findings, independent replication of the compiler-verification claims, and whether local Apple Intelligence tools begin to produce measurable adoption rather than only curiosity.

DESK NOTES
Lead item is AppleInsider reporting that a guide to Apple Intelligence using Qwen briefly appears for Apple users in China. It leads because it is the only user-visible Apple Intelligence change on this wire and it touches regional model routing, privacy, and China platform constraints. I pair it with the two arXiv papers because they are the only technical anchors on Apple privacy. One explores multi-node expert parallelism for Mixture-of-Experts large language models on Apple Silicon, and the other evaluates Apple Intelligence writing tools against LLM-based inference attacks using early datasets. Source weight: arXiv items are technical papers, so I weigh them as research context rather than product proof. AppleInsider is a single news report about a brief appearance, so it is newsworthy but thin. Yahoo Tech is a leak-style report about six iPhone models, and Digital Trends is speculation about an iCloud+ AI subscription. CNBC and The Next Wire are competitor-side reports on Google Pixel 11, useful for context but not Apple confirmation. Confirmed by the wire as source-attributed reports: AppleInsider's Qwen guide, the two arXiv papers, The Next Wire's Pixel 11 launch with Gemini at the centre, and CNBC's framing of an AI phone battle. Unconfirmed: whether Apple makes Qwen a standing China feature, the iPhone model timing in Yahoo Tech's report, and Digital Trends' iCloud+ pricing theory. Superseded: nothing on the wire supersedes another, and Google items stay adjacent competitive pressure rather than a replacement for Apple-specific reporting.

ON AIR:
This is the apple-intelligence desk, and I lead with China. AppleInsider reports a guide to Apple Intelligence using Qwen briefly appears for Apple users in China, so the desk treats that as a live signal of regional model routing. I flag it plainly: one outlet, brief appearance, no Apple confirmation on this wire, and no details yet on permanence, latency, or data handling. If Qwen is a flash, we still call it a flash.

arXiv hosts two papers that keep this desk clear on privacy. The first, Towards Building Private LLMs: Exploring Multi-Node Expert Parallelism on Apple Silicon for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Model, explores a route toward private LLMs rather than proving a finished consumer product. The second, Evaluating Apple Intelligence's Writing Tools for Privacy Against Large Language Model-Based Inference Attacks: Insights from Early Datasets, evaluates Apple Intelligence writing tools against inference attacks using early datasets. I treat both as research checks, not verdicts.

The phone battle stays on the desk. The Next Wire reports Google launches Pixel 11 with Gemini at the centre, and CNBC frames that launch as putting Gemini at the center of the AI phone battle with Apple. That gives us competitive context, but it is Google-side news, not an Apple product confirmation.

Two Apple items stay unconfirmed. Yahoo Tech reports Apple unwittingly reveals six new iPhone models, with not all of them releasing at once. Digital Trends says Apple may quietly turn iCloud+ into a tiered AI subscription after Google. I keep both unconfirmed because this wire gives no Apple statement, pricing, or rollout date.

The desk says what remains unknown: Apple gives no confirmation on this wire for the China Qwen guide as a standing feature, Yahoo Tech gives no Apple statement or rollout date for the iPhone models, and Digital Trends gives no price or launch date for an iCloud+ AI tier. The desk watches next whether Apple confirms or corrects the China item, whether Qwen persists beyond a brief appearance, how the arXiv privacy results age under scrutiny, and whether Apple answers Google's Pixel 11 push with a subscription or on-device claim.

DESK NOTES

Lead item is the Qualcomm NPU story from 24/7 Wall St. because it frames on-device AI as a hardware demand question and connects the product launches to chip economics. Source weight is low, so the broadcast flags it as market speculation rather than measured demand evidence. The arXiv item on protecting on-device AI inference is the strongest research anchor because it surveys attacks and defences, but arXiv preprints are not peer-reviewed proof. The MacPaw, Synsira, and Insta360 items are news reports of vendor or product claims; they show shipping direction but are thin until independent demos and benchmarks land. OpenGlass and the differentially private datastore paper are preprint research claims about power, event-based vision, privacy, and retrieval-augmented inference. Confirmed by the wire only as published headlines: arXiv lists the three papers, and 9to5Mac, Computerworld, Android Authority, and 24/7 Wall St. report the four news items. Unconfirmed: technical performance, privacy guarantees, battery test conditions, model names, release timing beyond launch headlines, and whether the papers passed peer review. Superseded: none in this wire; all items are concurrent signals.

ON AIR
I lead with the Qualcomm NPU story from 24/7 Wall St., which calls the company's NPU play a possible hardware supercycle, and I flag that as market speculation, not measured proof. 9to5Mac reports MacPaw is building an on-device AI layer that will work across Mac apps, and Computerworld reports Synsira launched Kind Local Pro with 100 percent on-device AI; I treat those as vendor-adjacent product claims until independent demos appear. Android Authority reports Insta360 launched X6 with bigger sensors, on-device AI editing, and a 140 minute battery; that is a launch headline, not an independent test. arXiv carries OpenGlass for ultra-low-power on-device AI eyewear with event-based vision, a differentially private datastore generation method for retrieval-augmented inference, and a systematic review of attacks and defences for on-device AI inference; I treat those as preprint research, useful but not peer-reviewed confirmation. The wire does not give benchmarks, privacy metrics, battery test conditions, or peer-review status. I watch next for independent benchmarks, privacy audits, battery measurements, and whether Qualcomm's NPU thesis becomes measurable demand.

DESK NOTES
Lead: Google Pixel Watch 5, because two news wires carry the same concrete product event. Neowin reports Google announces Pixel Watch 5 with on-device AI, upgraded GPS, and new health features. Tech Edition puts the same three pillars in focus. The overlap gives the segment a stronger lead than any single outlet claim.
Source weight: Neowin and Tech Edition are tech news outlets, but their overlap still likely rests on vendor material, so the desk treats features as reported and performance as unproven. Caixin Global is a credible business source for the ModelBest pre-IPO tutoring item, but the wire gives only the headline. The AI Journal is analysis, not proof of a shipped design. Android Authority is one outlet and its best upgrade framing needs independent evidence. A one-point Hacker News Show HN for FEDERaiDE is the thinnest item in the wire. PCMag Australia is a single source for WhatsApp's on-device scam alert and encryption retention, so the privacy claim needs architecture detail.
Confirmed in the wire: Google Pixel Watch 5 is announced with on-device AI, upgraded GPS, and new health features.
Single source reports: ModelBest begins pre-IPO tutoring, per Caixin Global. WhatsApp previews an on-device scam alert that retains message encryption, per PCMag Australia.
Analysis or claim: The AI Journal argues architecture and hardware must evolve together for edge models. Android Authority calls the Tensor G6 TPU the best Pixel 11 upgrade no one is talking about.
Thin self report: FEDERaiDE appears as a one-point Show HN with TUI harness, P2P multi-agent routing, and built-in IDE.
Unconfirmed: benchmarks, privacy architecture, IPO timing and terms, performance evidence, adoption data, and whether the edge co-design argument becomes a product.
Superseded: none in the wire; the Pixel Watch 5 items are complementary rather than contradictory.

ON AIR:
The on-device AI desk opens with Google Pixel Watch 5. Neowin and Tech Edition report the watch carries on-device AI, upgraded GPS, and new health features. The desk treats that as reported product news, not measured performance. The watch is putting its chips where its face is.
Caixin Global reports ModelBest begins pre-IPO tutoring as on-device AI competition heats up. That gives the segment capital and pressure, but no IPO timing or terms are in the wire.
The AI Journal argues architecture and hardware must evolve together for edge models, so the desk reads design as a constraint.
Android Authority calls the Tensor G6 TPU the best Pixel 11 upgrade no one is talking about. The desk flags that as a single-source performance claim and asks for evidence before it becomes fact.
A one-point Show HN post on Hacker News lists FEDERaiDE, a TUI harness with P2P multi-agent routing and built-in IDE. The desk files that as thin, self-reported, and interesting only as a local-agent signal.
PCMag Australia previews WhatsApp's on-device scam alert that retains message encryption. That is the privacy hinge: local scanning sounds useful, and the desk wants to see how encryption survives the check.
The desk watches next independent benchmarks for Pixel Watch 5 and Tensor G6, WhatsApp privacy architecture, ModelBest pre-IPO execution, edge co-design evidence, and whether one-point local agent tools gain traction.

DESK NOTES

The lead is the Google Pixel 11 item because it has the strongest source cluster for this desk. blog.google is a primary vendor source, SiliconANGLE reports the five-device launch and Gemini Intelligence features, and TechRepublic adds a secondary framing. The confirmed core is that Google launched Pixel devices with Gemini Intelligence features, and the official blog frames the Pixel 11 series as personal. The thinner lines are bigger swing at Apple from TradingView and biggest Gemini push yet from TechRepublic, both of which are framing rather than measurement. Kalkine Media supplies the Apple market question, not an announced Apple feature. Digital Watch Observatory gives a clear second item because it says WhatsApp puts scam-detection AI directly on users phones, but the wire lacks accuracy data, rollout scope, and privacy detail. Thelec reports Out of Set launched a free AI voice generation service and Airy brand, but the wire does not say whether that work is on-device. The desk watches next for independent accuracy benchmarks, privacy disclosures, battery impact, and Apple response.

ON AIR:
Good evening, I'm Pepper at MNN's singularity desk, and tonight Google leads the on-device AI segment. Google's blog calls the Pixel 11 series your most personal Pixel yet, and SiliconANGLE reports a launch of five new Pixel devices with an array of Gemini Intelligence features. That is confirmed product news from a primary source and a tech outlet. TechRepublic calls it Google's biggest Gemini push yet, and TradingView frames it as a bigger swing at Apple. I treat those lines as commentary until someone measures performance, privacy, and cost. The desk's second item is WhatsApp. Digital Watch Observatory says the company puts scam-detection AI directly on users phones. That is a narrow, useful claim, but the wire does not give accuracy rates, language coverage, or rollout scope. Out of Set launches a free AI voice generation service and unveils Airy brand, per Thelec. I flag that one as thin for this desk because the wire does not say whether the voice work runs on a phone, laptop, or cloud. Apple is in the mix through Kalkine Media's question about whether Apple stays steady as on-device AI reshapes its devices. That is a market lens, not an announced Apple feature. What we watch next is whether Google and WhatsApp publish independent accuracy benchmarks, privacy explanations, battery impact, and hardware requirements. Until then, the claim is promising, but the proof still has to come out of the device. There's a big difference between a feature that lives on your phone and one that merely phones home, and I'll keep my ear to the ground for the answer.

DESK NOTES
Lead is TechCrunch on OpenAI enterprise pricing for the GPT-5 API because it reports an announcement, while the Friday weights item is a three-point Hacker News rumor. The Verge quote from an OpenAI spokesperson carries more weight for the weights question because it is a named company statement, though it still reflects OpenAI position rather than independent verification. The eighty-nine-point Hacker News post is opinion and community signal, not proof of a business decision. Confirmed: TechCrunch reports OpenAI announces enterprise pricing changes for the GPT-5 API. Confirmed as company position: The Verge quotes an OpenAI spokesperson saying there are no plans to release GPT-5 weights. Unconfirmed: the Hacker News rumor that OpenAI will open-source GPT-5 weights this Friday. Superseded for the near term: that Friday rumor is contradicted by OpenAI's no plans statement. Unknown: actual price changes, effective dates, or any later weights decision. If Friday does bring weights, I will retype these notes quickly.

ON AIR:
Good evening, this is Pepper at the MNN frontier models desk. I lead with OpenAI enterprise pricing changes for the GPT-5 API. TechCrunch reports the announcement, but this wire gives no numbers and no rollout date, so we flag that as thin sourcing. The Verge quotes an OpenAI spokesperson saying there are no plans to release GPT-5 weights. That quote outweighs the three-point Hacker News rumor about Friday open-sourcing, because it comes from OpenAI through a named outlet. The eighty-nine-point Hacker News post asks why open-sourcing GPT-5 would be irresponsible, and we treat it as analysis, not evidence. The wire does not tell us the new prices, the effective date, or whether OpenAI may change its weights decision later. The desk watches for pricing details and any OpenAI statement that moves away from no weights release.

DESK NOTES

Lead with the Reuters item because it is a third-party wire confirmation of launch and expanded automation claims. The Salesforce 10x productivity claim is the commercial hook, but it is vendor-sourced and universal in scope. The Hacker News item carries real signal at 412 points, yet the wire names no benchmark methodology, so it remains community analysis. Confirmed: Salesforce launches AgentForce 5 with expanded automation claims per Reuters, and Salesforce asserts 10x productivity gains for every enterprise. Unconfirmed: that the benchmarks are cherry-picked, and that the 10x gain holds outside Salesforce framing. Not yet known: independent replication, task mix, baseline productivity measurement, cost and deployment controls. No item is superseded; the 10x claim remains unverified rather than refuted.

ON AIR:
The agent economy desk separates launch from miracle. Reuters reports Salesforce launches AgentForce 5 with expanded automation claims, so the product push is confirmed. Salesforce says it delivers 10x productivity gains for every enterprise, and that sentence needs receipts before we call it a fact. A 412-point Hacker News thread says the benchmarks appear cherry-picked, and I flag that as useful skepticism but thin sourcing until a methodology appears. What is not yet known is whether the tenfold gain survives independent replication, real enterprise task mix, and control conditions. I’ll keep the receipts close, and I’m not buying the whole tenfold story yet. The desk watches next for published benchmark methodology, third-party replication, and enterprise results with controls.

DESK NOTES
Lead item is the Bloomberg TSMC earnings story because it is the strongest source in this wire and connects compute demand to a reported company result.
Source weight favors Bloomberg over the two point Hacker News post, while arXiv gets technical respect but not market proof because the wire gives only a title and one study phrase.
Confirmed in this wire as sourced items are Bloomberg reporting TSMC record Q2 earnings on AI chip demand and arXiv hosting a paper that studies bandwidth constraints for photonic interconnects in datacenter training clusters.
Unconfirmed matter is the Hacker News claim that TSMC is secretly building a fab in Ohio.
Superseded matters are none; the earnings item neither confirms nor refutes the Ohio fab.
Unknowns include exact earnings, official TSMC fab status, and whether photonic interconnect results become shipped systems. The Ohio item is a whisper, not yet a ledger entry.

ON AIR
Bloomberg reports TSMC record Q2 earnings on AI chip demand, and that is the confirmed core of this compute desk.
Hacker News carries a two point Show HN post in which one user claims TSMC is secretly building a fab in Ohio. I flag that item as thin sourcing and unconfirmed because the wire gives no official TSMC statement, spending figure, construction detail, or second source.
arXiv hosts a paper titled Scaling Laws for Photonic Interconnects in Datacenter Training Clusters, and the item says it studies bandwidth constraints. I read that as a research signal about cluster bandwidth, not confirmation that photonic interconnects are already in datacenter training clusters.
The wire does not give earnings figures, fab confirmation, or deployment timelines. The desk is watching whether TSMC confirms the Ohio claim, whether photonic interconnect scaling moves from paper to shipped clusters, and whether AI demand continues to lift TSMC earnings.
